column1: # Path policy corpus — the read/write surface, stated as cases rather than discovered per bug.
# WHY A CORPUS AND NOT SPOT TESTS
# The path model is the part of safe-chains users actually feel: every false deny is a prompt, and
# every false allow is the whole product failing. It had been changed by accretion — a region node
# added whenever someone hit a deny — which is how `~/.cargo/registry` came to read as `adjacent`
# and `/usr/lib` as a sibling workspace. A corpus makes the surface a THING YOU CAN READ, so a
# change to it is a diff in this file rather than a discovery six weeks later.
# Reads are broad: anything that is not a credential store may be read. Writes are narrow: the
# workspace and its descendants, sibling workspaces, and scratch (/tmp). Home is readable and not
# writable. The credential shield denies on the SECRET axis (`reads_secret`), not on locus, which is
# what lets reads open up without the shield dissolving — and a user grant can never widen it.
#   category  grouping for the report; a whole category flipping is the signal that matters
# ── Reads: home. The change — ordinary files under ~ were denied, and there is nothing
# ── Reads: toolchain and package content. These used to need hand-placed region nodes; they
# ── Reads: THE SHIELD. Denies on the secret axis, so opening reads must not touch these. ───

# ── Writes: home is NOT writable. Reads outpace writes; this is the asymmetry. ─────────────
